clue.text: See "representative"

parts.note: a see is a bishop's seat, here the Holy See, and the clue asks for its envoy abroad

explanation.surface: A cross-reference telling the reader to look up the word 'representative'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a cross-reference instruction, but it is the Holy See, the papacy, whose diplomatic representative is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A papal ambassador accredited to a foreign government represents the Holy See.

clue.text: Wife of famous hero buried here. Buried alive

indicators.note: the answer lies buried inside the words famous hero, spanning the join

explanation.surface: A grave marker announcing where the wife of a celebrated hero lies.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'famoUS HERo'. In Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher', Madeline Usher is entombed while still alive, which is how the name defines 'Buried alive'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's heroine Madeline, of the family in 'The Fall of the House of', is interred while still living.

clue.text: McLuhan felt it to be our business

definitions.text: McLuhan felt it to be our business

parts.words: McLuhan felt it to be our business
parts.note: the title of Marshall McLuhan's 1970 book is the phrase 'our business' completes

explanation.surface: A remark about what the media theorist Marshall McLuhan thought we should be doing.
explanation.definitionFit: Marshall McLuhan's 1970 book title names arts and civilisation as our business.

clue.text: Illyrian duke shows alternative to vice ring

parts.note: the word 'or' introduces an alternative
a vice is a sin
a ring is the round letter O

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean duke shows a choice other than wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke of Illyria is the lovesick ruler in Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night' is set in Illyria, ruled by this lovesick nobleman.

clue.text: Virginia Woolf wrote on his death bed

definitions.text: Virginia Woolf wrote on his death bed

parts.words: Virginia Woolf wrote on his death bed
parts.note: the clue recalls the title of a posthumous Woolf essay collection about a ship's commander's last bed

explanation.surface: An image of Virginia Woolf writing while someone lies dying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Captain's Death Bed' is a 1950 collection of Woolf's essays; the clue reads as if she wrote at a bedside.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's essay collection is titled after the death bed of a ship's commander.

clue.text: Composer is poet and novelist

parts.note: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, the Romantic poet
Elizabeth Taylor, the English novelist

explanation.surface: A claim that one musician is both a poet and a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor was an English composer, best known for 'Hiawatha's Wedding Feast'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor wrote the cantata 'Hiawatha's Wedding Feast'.

clue.text: Charrier's dog?

parts.note: Henri Charriere's memoir shares its name with a toy spaniel breed named for its butterfly ears

explanation.surface: A question about a pet belonging to someone called Charrier.
explanation.walkthrough: Henri Charriere wrote the memoir of his escape from French Guiana under his nickname, which is also a breed of small dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Charriere's nickname and memoir title is also a toy spaniel breed with butterfly-shaped ears.

clue.text: Arabella Winklepicker

parts.note: read as Arabella, the girl Mr Winkle picked in Dickens's 'Pickwick Papers', giving her surname

explanation.surface: A woman called Arabella with a pointed-toe shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: A winklepicker is a pointed shoe, but here it means the one Winkle picks: Arabella, sister of Benjamin, whom Nathaniel Winkle marries in 'The Pickwick Papers'.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'The Pickwick Papers' Arabella's maiden surname is that of her medical-student brother Ben.

clue.text: Dramatist on abstract painter

explanation.surface: A playwright placed on top of a modern artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname shared by the playwright of 'Shadowlands' and the abstract artist Ben, husband of Barbara Hepworth.

clue.text: Bang of bell spurred the halfmile wheelmen to their sprint" (James Joyce, Ulysses)

definitions.text: Bang of bell spurred the halfmile wheelmen to their sprint" (James Joyce, Ulysses)

parts.words: Bang of bell spurred the halfmile wheelmen to their sprint" (James Joyce, Ulysses)
parts.note: a quotation from Ulysses with three words missing between 'of' and 'bell'

explanation.surface: A line from Joyce's 'Ulysses' about a cycle race.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyce wrote 'Bang of the last lap bell spurred the halfmile wheelmen to their sprint'; the missing words go between 'of' and 'bell'.
explanation.definitionFit: In a cycle race a bell signals the final circuit, which spurs riders to sprint.

clue.text: Macheath could have been happy with her

definitions.text: Macheath could have been happy with her

parts.words: Macheath could have been happy with her
parts.note: Macheath sings 'How happy could I be with either' of his two loves, Polly and the jailer's daughter

explanation.surface: A remark that the highwayman Macheath might have found contentment with a certain woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gay's 'The Beggar's Opera' Macheath sings 'How happy could I be with either' of Polly Peachum and Lockit's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockit's daughter in 'The Beggar's Opera' is one of the two women Macheath could be happy with.

clue.text: Odin was lord of this ring

definitions.text: Odin was lord of this ring

parts.words: Odin was lord of this ring
parts.note: a nod to Tolkien's title, pointing to the gold ring of Norse myth owned by Odin

explanation.surface: A statement that the Norse god Odin was master of a ring, echoing Tolkien.
explanation.walkthrough: In Norse myth Odin owns a gold ring that drips eight more rings every ninth night; 'lord of this ring' echoes Tolkien.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse mythology gives Odin a self-multiplying gold arm-ring forged by dwarfs.

clue.text: Poet offers pound and gold

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A poet hands over money and gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Savage Landor was an English poet. L (from Latin libra) is the pound sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Savage Landor was an English writer of verse and 'Imaginary Conversations'.

clue.text: Created with crown by O'Casey

parts.note: the title of a volume of Sean O'Casey's autobiography pairs a flower with a crown, and 'created' hints that the word also means ...

explanation.surface: A remark that O'Casey made something with a crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose and Crown' (1952) is a volume of O'Casey's autobiography; the past tense of 'rise' fits 'created' only loosely, as in arose or came into being.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Casey's autobiographical volume pairs this flower with a crown, like an English pub sign.

clue.text: No oil painting, and may make gaoler hop

indicators.note: the letters of gaoler and hop may be made into something new by rearranging them

explanation.surface: An unflattering verdict on someone's looks, and a scene of a jailer made to jump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No oil painting' usually means plain-looking; here it is literal: a lithograph printed to imitate an oil painting. 'may make' rearranges GAOLER HOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A print in oil colours imitating an oil painting is only an imitation of one.

clue.text: Like one of Burgess's hooligans

parts.note: Anthony Burgess's teenage thugs in 'A Clockwork Orange' are called by a Nadsat word, here made an adjective

explanation.surface: Describing behaviour like a thug from an Anthony Burgess novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'A Clockwork Orange', Alex and his gang call themselves by a Nadsat word from Russian drug, friend; the answer adds -ish.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgess's gang of young thugs use a Russian-derived word for 'friend' as their name; the adjective describes their manner.

clue.text: Illume gig in order to see opera composer

indicators.note: the letters of illume and gig are put in order, rearranged to give the name

explanation.surface: An instruction to light up a performance to see an operatic composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Pietro Alessandro Guglielmi was an 18th-century Italian opera composer. 'in order' rearranges ILLUME GIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Pietro Guglielmi wrote about a hundred Italian comic operas in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Cockpit re-opened by this poet laureate

definitions.text: Cockpit re-opened by this poet laureate

parts.words: Cockpit re-opened by this poet laureate
parts.note: the Cockpit was a London theatre which a Stuart laureate reopened for opera during the Commonwealth

explanation.surface: An aircraft cockpit reopened by a poet laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cockpit was a Drury Lane theatre; Sir William Davenant staged opera there in 1658 when plays were banned.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir William Davenant, laureate under Charles I, staged entertainments at the Cockpit theatre in Drury Lane.

clue.text: Prizewinning poet Sara suggests beverages with lady diarist

parts.note: teas are hot drinks
Mrs Dale of the BBC radio serial 'Mrs Dale's Diary'

explanation.surface: A poet's name suggests drinks taken with a woman who keeps a diary.
explanation.walkthrough: Sara Teasdale won the first Pulitzer Prize for poetry in 1918. 'Mrs Dale's Diary' was a long-running British radio soap, so Dale is the lady diarist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sara Teasdale, American lyric poet, won a 1918 Pulitzer for 'Love Songs'.

clue.text: One of these was for sale in Greeneland

definitions.text: One of these was for sale in Greeneland

parts.words: One of these was for sale in Greeneland
parts.note: Greeneland is the world of Graham Greene's novels, one of which offers a firearm for sale in its title

explanation.surface: Something was on sale in a land called Greeneland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greeneland' is critics' name for Graham Greene's fictional world; his novel 'A Gun for Sale' supplies the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Greene's thriller 'A Gun for Sale' names one firearm on the market.

clue.text: Southern writer with presidential connection?

parts.note: the Southern writer's first name is the surname of President Harry Truman

explanation.surface: A question about an author from the American South linked to a president.
explanation.walkthrough: Truman Capote, from New Orleans and Alabama, shares a first name with President Harry S. Truman.
explanation.definitionFit: Truman Capote, born in New Orleans, wrote 'In Cold Blood' and 'Breakfast at Tiffany's'.

clue.text: A German title, for example, of Alamein

parts.note: a title is a name

explanation.surface: A German honorific, such as the one taken from the battle of Alamein.
explanation.walkthrough: An agname is an extra name earned by deeds, like Montgomery's 'of Alamein'.
explanation.definitionFit: Montgomery's 'of Alamein' is an additional name earned for a deed, the kind Romans called a cognomen.

clue.text: Conrad's secret

parts.note: Joseph Conrad's novel title pairs the adjective secret with the spy it describes

explanation.surface: Something Joseph Conrad kept hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad's 1907 novel is 'The Secret Agent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad's novel is about a spy, a secret operative named in its title.

clue.text: Muses' spring might supply pep again.

indicators.note: the letters of pep again might supply the name when rearranged

explanation.surface: A spring of the Muses might restore your energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Aganippe is the spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses. 'might supply' rearranges PEP AGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Aganippe is the fountain on Mount Helicon sacred to the nine goddesses of the arts.

clue.text: Father with the foremost in slow dance

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
the van is the foremost part of an army or procession

explanation.surface: Dad and the leaders take part in a stately dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The pavan is a slow processional court dance of the sixteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately processional court dance of Renaissance Europe.

clue.text: … Spring offered its stimulus

parts.note: a continuation of the Muses' spring clue, recalling Milton's line that this is the spur

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the spring gave its encouragement.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis continues 23 across: the Muses' spring offered the spur. Milton's 'Lycidas' says 'Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton calls renown 'the spur that the clear spirit doth raise' in 'Lycidas'.

clue.text: Written by Dryden for no other reward?

definitions.text: Written by Dryden for no other reward?

parts.words: Written by Dryden for no other reward?
parts.note: the title of Dryden's Antony and Cleopatra tragedy also means writing purely out of affection

explanation.surface: A suggestion that Dryden wrote without any payment.
explanation.walkthrough: Dryden's 1677 tragedy on Antony and Cleopatra is 'All for Love'; the phrase also means for no reward but affection.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryden's tragedy title also means doing something purely out of affection, not payment.

clue.text: Brecht's coach

parts.note: Brecht adapted Lenz's 'Der Hofmeister', whose English title names a private teacher

explanation.surface: A coach belonging to Bertolt Brecht.
explanation.walkthrough: Brecht adapted Lenz's 'Der Hofmeister', known in English as 'The Tutor'; 'coach' means private teacher, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach is a private teacher, the title figure of Brecht's adaptation of Lenz.

clue.text: Followers of apparently somewhat sheepish literary lion

definitions.text: Followers of apparently somewhat sheepish literary lion

parts.words: Followers of apparently somewhat sheepish literary lion
parts.note: the sheepish lion is Charles Lamb, whose essays appeared under the pen-name Elia

explanation.surface: Fans of a famous writer who seems rather timid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheepish' points to Charles Lamb, the literary lion who wrote as Elia; his admirers are named after the pen-name.
explanation.definitionFit: Admirers of Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia' are named after his pen-name.
